subject: Transportation Systems
title: Track Geometry at 200 mph
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Track Geometry at 200 mph.

hook.text: At 200 mph, a flaw in the track one millimeter too large can cause a derailment.

buildup.text: High-speed track is welded into continuous ribbons of steel—no gaps, no joints, no jolts.

discovery.text: Slab track—concrete instead of ballast—holds geometry to sub-millimeter precision for decades.

twist.text: Slab track costs twice as much to build but barely needs maintenance. Ballasted track needs constant adjusting.

climax.text: Special measurement trains scan tracks weekly, detecting deformations invisible to the human eye.

punchline.text: At 200 mph, the track matters more than the train.

quiz.question: Why do high-speed lines often use slab track instead of ballast?
options: It holds geometry to sub-millimeter precision with less maintenance
